That changes the serving stack and a few key config details — and the reassuring part: **all the instrumentation I built for the original Qwen transfer row is exactly what this needs.** The parse-retry/repair counting, the `quote_match` mechanical-vs-semantic flip decomposition, `model_override`, and model-in-cache-key (DECISIONS 23–26) were built anticipating this model. The integration is genuinely small. And Qwen-as-local-primary collapses three goals into one model: unlimited (no rate limit), self-hosted (data sovereignty), **and cross-family** (Alibaba, not Google — recovering what the Gemma swap would have cost).

Here's the revised strategy, as deltas from the Gemma/Ollama plan.

## What Qwen 3.6 35B A3B actually is (and the one hard constraint)

MoE: **35B total / 3B active**, 256 experts (8 routed + 1 shared), hybrid attention, 262K context, Apache-2.0, text+vision ([Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), [vLLM recipe](https://recipes.vllm.ai/Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B)). The MoE part is great for you — only 3B params compute per token, so inference is fast (a GPTQ-Int4 of the sibling 3.5 runs ~195 tok/s on a 5090).

**The constraint: MoE reduces *compute*, not *memory* — all 35B params must be VRAM-resident.** So on the 32GB 5090, quantization isn't optional:

| quant | size | fits 32GB? |
|---|---|---|
| BF16 | ~70GB | ✗ |
| FP8 (`Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8`) | ~35GB | ✗ (just over) |
| **NVFP4 (`nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4`)** | **~18–20GB** | **✓ — and Blackwell-native FP4** |
| GPTQ-Int4 | ~18–20GB | ✓ (portable fallback) |

**Pick `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4`** ([HF](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4)) — the 5090's FP4 tensor cores make this the quality+speed sweet spot, and ~18GB leaves comfortable room for KV cache. FP8 is *just* too big for 32GB; note 4-bit as a logged quality caveat for the headline (same discipline as reasoning-off was).

## Serving: vLLM from HF weights (the "HuggingFace config" path)

vLLM loads the HF checkpoint directly and exposes the OpenAI-compatible server — the right fit over Ollama now that you want HF weights. The canonical setup is the [vLLM Qwen3.6 recipe](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/recipes/en/latest/Qwen/Qwen3.5.html); pin the vLLM version it specifies (Blackwell sm_120 + NVFP4 kernels need a recent build — this is the one fiddly part, same caveat as before: CUDA 12.8+, `VLLM_FLASH_ATTN_VERSION=2` if FA3 errors).

```bash
docker run -d --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  -e VLLM_FLASH_ATTN_VERSION=2 \
  vllm/vllm-openai:<blackwell-capable-tag> \
  --model nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --served-model-name qwen3.6-35b-a3b \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}' \
  --max-model-len 16384 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90
```

Key choices: `--max-model-len 16384` (our transcripts render to ~8k; no need for 262K — saves KV VRAM); `--served-model-name qwen3.6-35b-a3b` becomes the `model_override` string and flows into cache keys; mount the HF cache so the ~18GB download persists. Qwen is ungated (Apache-2.0), so no HF token needed.

## The Qwen-specific config detail: thinking control via chat template

This is the main integration delta. Gemini used `reasoning_effort: none`; **Qwen3's thinking toggle lives in the chat template** — `enable_thinking: false` ([vLLM reasoning docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/reasoning_outputs/), [Qwen-3.5 no-thinking writeup](https://medium.com/@ishaafsalman/run-qwen3-5-9b-with-vllm-streaming-no-thinking-mode-ff19bb4ab51f)). Two ways, and our `extra_body` passthrough already handles the per-request form:

- Server-wide: the `--default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'` flag above.
- Per-request (belt-and-suspenders): `extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}}`.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about NVFP4 quantization setup for vLLM and TensorRT-LLM on RTX 50 series GPUs:

## NVFP4 Overview

NVFP4 is a 4-bit floating-point format introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs to maintain model accuracy while reducing memory bandwidth and storage requirements for inference workloads. NVFP4 is NVIDIA's 4-bit floating-point format for Blackwell GPUs (SM100+).

## Hardware Support

GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs boast fifth-generation Tensor Cores with 4-bit floating point compute (FP4). NVFP4 requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (SM100+ for quantization, SM100/SM120 for inference).

## Deployment Frameworks

Once quantized, the NVFP4 model can be easily exported to a Unified Hugging Face Checkpoint and deployed on NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, which offers early NVFP4 support.

## Setup Requirements & Model Optimizer

For quantization using TensorRT Model Optimizer:
- You can quantize models using NVIDIA's TensorRT Model Optimizer inside a TensorRT-LLM container, producing an NVFP4 quantized model for deployment.
- The conversion process requires huge amounts of RAM (>100GB). If you have "only" 64GB RAM, you need a massive SWAP file.

## Performance Benefits

Combined with Blackwell's native NVFP4 tensor cores, memory bandwidth usage is slashed by ~50% vs FP8, allowing the card to hit extremely high token rates usually reserved for 7B models. Dense 30B models in FP8 typically hit 60-80 t/s, while this setup is ~2x faster.

## Pre-quantized Models

Hugging Face already hosts NVFP4 prequantized checkpoints ready for deployment, including some of the most popular: DeepSeek-R1-0528, Llama 3, and FLUX.1-dev.

Yes — and you're not on the edge of *capability*, only of *software maturity*. The RTX 5090 has 5th-gen tensor cores with native FP4 compute (sm_120), which is precisely what NVFP4 targets, and there's direct confirmation people run **Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in NVFP4 on a single 32GB 5090 via vLLM** ([dasroot writeup](https://dasroot.net/posts/2026/04/unlocking-nvfp4-speed-consumer-gpus/), [Li-Lee/vllm-qwen3.5-nvfp4-5090](https://github.com/Li-Lee/vllm-qwen3.5-nvfp4-5090)). NVFP4 weights ≈ 18GB, so it fits with comfortable KV-cache room, and it ~halves memory bandwidth vs FP8 for roughly 2× the token rate ([NVIDIA NVFP4 blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/introducing-nvfp4-for-efficient-and-accurate-low-precision-inference/)).

**What it takes:**
- **Use a pre-quantized checkpoint** (`nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4`) — do *not* quantize it yourself. ModelOptimizer conversion wants >100GB RAM; with your 64GB you'd be swapping hard. Pre-quant skips that entirely.
- **vLLM `:nightly` image, not `:latest`** — nightly ships PyTorch kernels compiled for sm_120, which is what the 5090 needs; stable lags. Driver ~**580.95.05**, CUDA 12.8+.

**The one honest landmine — and it's specific to your model:** NVFP4 **MoE** on *consumer* Blackwell (sm_120) is the bleeding edge. There's an open vLLM failure — "No NvFp4 MoE backend supports the deployment configuration" — on a Nemotron-30B-**A3B**-NVFP4, which is also an MoE ([vLLM #35065](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/35065)), and the TensorRT-LLM path needs community C++ patches to run 30B MoE NVFP4 on a 5090 ([trtllm-nvfp4-blackwell-fix](https://github.com/JohnTDI-cpu/trtllm-nvfp4-blackwell-fix)). Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is an MoE, so budget for possibly hitting this on first boot — it's the MoE+NVFP4+sm_120 combination that's fragile, not NVFP4 itself.

**Your no-drama fallback:** a **GPTQ-Int4 or AWQ-Int4** checkpoint of the same model. Int4 is mature on the 5090 today — the sibling `Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4` runs at ~195 tok/s on one ([HF discussion](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4/discussions/3)). Same ~18GB footprint, doesn't use the FP4 cores (slightly slower), but it just works.

**For *our* purpose, the choice barely matters.** We run sequential, low-concurrency, ~1,300 calls total — token throughput is not the constraint (no rate limit is the whole point). NVFP4's 2× speed is irrelevant to us; what matters is *quality* and *that it boots*. NVFP4 preserves accuracy better than naive Int4 (two-level microblock scaling), so it's the nicer pick **if it starts** — but if the MoE backend fights you for more than a short while, drop to GPTQ-Int4 and lose nothing that matters for this experiment. Either way, the quant level becomes a logged variable in DECISIONS (exactly as reasoning-off was).

So: **try `nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4` on vLLM nightly first; keep a GPTQ-Int4 checkpoint as the fallback.** Both fit your 32GB, both integrate identically into agentmon (the serving stack and client config are unchanged — only the `--model` path differs). The SSH config is set up correctly — but the reachability probe surfaced a useful diagnostic about the box itself.

**Config: done.** `~/.ssh/config` created (perms `600`, `~/.ssh` is `700`), resolving exactly as you specified: `omen → gh-user@192.0.2.10:22` with `LocalForward 8000 → localhost:8000`.

**The box is on, but sshd isn't running yet.** The probe got **"Connection refused"**, not a timeout — that distinction matters: a timeout would mean the host is down or the IP is wrong, but an active *refusal* means **192.0.2.10 is powered on and reachable on your LAN, but nothing is listening on port 22.** So the SSH server isn't up on the omen yet.

**Fix on the omen (Ubuntu), then we're connected:**
```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y openssh-server
sudo systemctl enable --now ssh
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp        # only if UFW is enabled
```

**Then, from this Mac:**

2. `ssh omen` — opens the session **and** the tunnel. Keep that terminal open during eval runs; agentmon's client points at `http://localhost:8000/v1`, which the tunnel carries to vLLM on the box.

Done on the Mac side — here's where it stands and the one command left for you.

**Created & configured (Mac):**
- Dedicated key `~/.ssh/id_ed25519_omen` (`600`) + `.pub` (`644`) — ed25519, no passphrase, scoped to omen only.

**The last step needs your omen password, so it's yours to run once** (I don't have it and shouldn't handle it). Either of these installs the public key on the box:

```bash

# Option B — paste into your already-open omen session:
```

**Two notes:**
- **Security tradeoff:** the key has no passphrase, which is what makes unattended eval runs frictionless, but anyone with read access to that file on your Mac could reach the omen. Yes — the `>>` is real bash syntax you must type, not an annotation. It's the **append** operator: it adds the quoted public-key line to the end of `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` (creating the file if it doesn't exist).

Important distinction: use `>>` (two), **not** `>` (one). A single `>` would *overwrite* the file — wiping any keys already in it. `>>` safely appends.

Everything else in that line is literal too — the single quotes around the key and the file path stay exactly as written. So the whole command is typed verbatim:

